title: Conditionals
summary: An if statement lets Python choose a step when a rule is true. An else part gives another path.
introduction: An if statement lets Python choose a step when a rule is true. An else part gives another path. A club might need different messages for a full or empty reading list. Try both cases and watch the spaces at the start of each line.
learningObjectives: Branch with if, elif and else and predict which block runs
Combine conditions with and, or and not, including chained comparisons
Write a conditional expression on one line
Use match to select among several structured cases

blocks.title: grade.py

blocks.text: Python tests the conditions from top to bottom and runs the *first* block whose condition is true, then skips the rest; the `else` block catches everything that remains. Order matters: if the `score >= 70` test came first, an 83 would be a C. `elif` and `else` are optional, and an `if` with neither is common.

rows: Less than, less or equal, greater than, greater or equal
Membership in a string, list, tuple, set or dict

blocks.title: compare.py
blocks.code:
age = 20
print(age == 20, age != 20)
print(age > 18, age <= 18)
print(18 <= age < 65)           # chained: both comparisons must hold
print("a" < "b", "apple" < "banana")
print("py" in "python", 3 in [1, 2, 3])
result = None
print(result is None, result is not None)

blocks.title: python compare.py
blocks.content:
True False
True False
True
True True
True True
True False

blocks.text: Chained comparisons read like mathematics: `18 <= age < 65` is true only when both halves are. Strings compare character by character using their Unicode code, so upper-case letters sort before lower-case ones. For `None` use `is` and `is not`: `is` asks whether two names refer to the *same object*, which is exactly the right question for singletons like `None`, `True` and `False`; for ordinary values stick to `==`.

blocks.title: logic.py
blocks.code:
is_member = True
age = 15
balance = 0

print(is_member and age >= 18)
print(is_member or age >= 18)
print(not is_member)

if balance:
    print("You have money")
else:
    print("Balance is zero")

name = ""
display = name or "Anonymous"
print(display)

blocks.title: python logic.py
blocks.content:
False
True
False
Balance is zero
Anonymous

blocks.text: `and` is true only when both sides are true, `or` when at least one is, and `not` flips a value. Python evaluates lazily and returns the deciding operand: `a or b` gives `a` if it is truthy, otherwise `b`, which is where the `name or "Anonymous"` idiom for default values comes from. `if balance:` relies on truthiness: zero, `None`, empty strings and empty collections count as false, everything else as true (see [Data Types](/tutorials/python/data-types)).

blocks.title: A condition that is always true
blocks.text: `if day == "Sat" or "Sun":` reads naturally but does not do what it says. Python evaluates `day == "Sat"`, then `"Sun"` on its own, and a non-empty string is always truthy, so the block runs for every day of the week. Write `if day == "Sat" or day == "Sun":` or, better, `if day in ("Sat", "Sun"):`.
When all you need is to choose between two *values*, an `if` block is heavy. The conditional expression `a if condition else b` fits on one line and can sit inside an f-string or a function call.

blocks.title: ternary.py
blocks.code:
temperature = 12
label = "warm" if temperature > 20 else "cold"
print(label)

items = 1
print(f"{items} item{'s' if items != 1 else ''}")

blocks.text: When one value must be compared with many possibilities, a chain of `elif`s works, but `match` (Python 3.10 and later) reads better. Each `case` is tried in order, `|` separates alternatives, and `_` is the wildcard that matches anything, so it plays the role of `else`.

blocks.title: status.py
blocks.code:
status = 404

match status:
    case 200:
        print("OK")
    case 301 | 302:
        print("Redirect")
    case 404:
        print("Not found")
    case _:
        print("Something else")

blocks.text: `match` can also pull values *out* of structured data. The patterns below match lists of a certain length and bind the pieces to names, so a tiny text-adventure parser needs no indexing at all:

blocks.title: command.py
blocks.code:
command = "go north"

match command.split():
    case ["go", direction]:
        print(f"Moving {direction}")
    case ["take", item]:
        print(f"Picking up the {item}")
    case ["quit"] | ["exit"]:
        print("Goodbye")
    case _:
        print("I do not understand")

blocks.text: Change `command` to `"take lamp"`, `"exit"` or `"dance"` and run it again to see the other branches. Capturing names such as `direction` are plain variables: the first pattern only matches a two-item list whose first item is `"go"`.

blocks.title: Keep conditions readable
blocks.text: Deeply nested `if` blocks are hard to follow. Give a complex condition a name (`is_eligible = age >= 18 and is_member`), handle the exceptional case first and leave the main path unindented, and reach for `match` once an `elif` chain compares the same value more than three times.

questions.question: What does this program print?
questions.explanation: Only the first true branch runs. `x > 5` is true, so `big` is printed and the `elif` is never tested, even though `x > 6` is also true.

questions.question: `if x == 1 or 2:` is true only when `x` is 1 or 2.
questions.explanation: The expression is `(x == 1) or 2`, and `2` is truthy, so the condition is true for every value of `x`. Write `x == 1 or x == 2` or `x in (1, 2)`.
